manifest.title: The Convincing Impostor: Alternating Depths
manifest.subtitle: Synthetic simulation of an eclipsing binary star exhibiting primary and secondary eclipses
manifest.segmentPolicy: Continuous simulation with single 2-day orbit downlink gap
preparationSteps: Generated box transit model with primary depth 2.5% and secondary depth 0.8%
Injected Gaussian photometric noise (sigma=1500 ppm, seed=42)
Inserted 2-day observational gap to simulate spacecraft downlink

teaching.learningGoal: Recognize why a convincing folded signal at half-period is actually an eclipsing binary star.
teaching.skillPracticed: Alternating depth test and harmonic period resolution
guidedQuestions: When folded at P = 2.10 days, the dips align cleanly. But look closely at the depth of alternating events. Are they identical?
What happens if you double the trial period to P = 4.20 days?
Why would a binary star system produce deep and shallow dips every other orbit?
teaching.explanationSummary: If folded at 2.10 days (half the true orbital period), primary and secondary eclipses fold together. However, checking the Alternating Depths evidence card exposes a statistically significant depth difference (2.5% vs 0.8%), proving this is a binary star system, not an exoplanet.

teacherAnswerReveal.astronomicalContext: Eclipsing binaries (EBs) are two stars orbiting their common center of mass.
teacherAnswerReveal.trueNature: Detached Eclipsing Binary Star (Primary Star + Secondary Star)
teacherAnswerReveal.evidenceEvaluation: When folded at P = 2.1 days, alternating depths differ significantly (>10σ). Doubling the period to P = 4.20 days shows a primary eclipse at phase 0.0 and a secondary eclipse at phase 0.5.
alternativeExplanations: Two separate planets with resonant periods (ruled out by identical durations and exact 2:1 period ratio).
Eclipsing binary with cooler secondary star (the correct astrophysical interpretation).
